query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (approximately 5–10 atomic percent) of HCP‐forming elements such as Ti or Zr to the equal‐atomic, BCC NbMoTaW alloy will enhance its room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving the BCC structural integrity and high-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with excellent high-temperature properties but limited room-temperature ductility and unproven irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Substitute or add 5–10 atomic percent of HCP-forming elements (e.g., Ti or Zr) into the NbMoTaW alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Tests at room temperature (for improved ductility), high temperature up to 1600 °C (to evaluate mechanical performance retention), and under irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation) to assess irradiation tolerance.
generation.structural_mediator: Subtle microstructural modifications, where the added HCP-forming elements reduce the dislocation core energy and modulate lattice distortion within a predominantly BCC matrix, potentially creating nanoscale heterogeneities that facilitate dislocation movement without full-scale phase transformation.
generation.mechanism: The incorporation of HCP-forming elements is expected to lower the energy barriers for dislocation movement (as evidenced in analogous RHEAs such as TiZrHfNbTa), thereby enhancing ductility. Simultaneously, the improved atomic diffusion and redistribution may promote self-healing under irradiation, mitigating irradiation-induced defects while largely maintaining the BCC structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the modified alloy should exhibit a higher room-temperature strain-to-failure (indicating improved ductility), retain high-temperature strength (with only minimal reduction), and demonstrate enhanced resistance to irradiation damage such as reduced amorphization or blistering under helium implantation conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW with high tensile strength at 1600 °C and limited ductility at room temperature, and computationally-inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable for alloys containing up to about 10 atomic percent of added HCP-forming elements, and the improvements are expected under room-temperature mechanical loading, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical testing, and under irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation regimes) that simulate operational environments.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise optimal concentration of HCP-forming elements needed and the quantitative extent to which irradiation tolerance improves. There is also uncertainty if any detrimental phase instability or segregation might occur at the proposed dopant levels.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW-based alloys with 0%, 5%, and 10% atomic substitution by Ti or Zr. Process all alloys under identical conditions to stabilize the single-phase BCC structure. Perform tensile tests at room temperature to measure ductility, conduct high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C to assess strength retention, and subject samples to controlled helium implantation to simulate irradiation effects.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance
Post-irradiation microstructural analysis (using TEM, XRD) to detect amorphization, blistering, or precipitation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloys show either a significant degradation in the BCC phase stability (e.g., transition to secondary phases or segregation) or no statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Intrinsic factors responsible for brittle versus ductile nature of refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: M
